title: Lesson 2 - Backpropagation and the Chain Rule
author: Sample course (bundled with the project)

segments.text: in the previous lesson we said that the gradient tells us which way is downhill. we did not say how
to compute it. that is what backpropagation does, and it is the subject of this lesson. backpropagation is the chain
rule applied systematically, from the output layer backwards to the input layer. you compute the error at the output, then
you ask how much each weight in the layer before contributed to that error, and you keep pushing that question
backwards through the network. the reason it is efficient is reuse. the intermediate results you need for one layer are
exactly the results you already computed for the layer after it, so nothing is calculated twice. without that reuse you
would need a separate pass for every single weight, which for a modern network is completely impractical. a common confusion
is between backpropagation and gradient descent. they are not the same thing. backpropagation computes the gradient. gradient descent is what
uses the gradient to update the weights, and the learning rate is what scales that update. one more practical point
before we finish. in practice nobody runs this over the whole dataset before taking a step. instead we use stochastic
gradient descent, estimating the gradient from a small batch of maybe thirty two or sixty four examples and stepping immediately.
the estimate is noisy but you take thousands of steps instead of one, and the noise actually helps you escape
